**Menachem Mendel Schneersohn – the third Rebbe of Chabad and author of *Derech Mitzvosecha* – followed the teachings and example of his father‑figure and mentor, Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi.**  

- Shneur Zalman was the founder of the Chabad‑Lubavitch Hasidic movement and the great‑grandfather’s teacher.  
- Schneersohn was raised by Shneur Zalman after his mother died and studied under him, taking to heart Shneur’s Chabad philosophy (“Chabad” = Chochma‑Bina‑Da’at).  
- In his own writings, Schneersohn repeatedly cites the *Tanya* and other works compiled by Shneur Zalman, showing that he followed and built upon his mentor’s ideas.  

So, the creator of *Derech Mitzvosecha* followed **Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi**.

_**Derech Mitzvosecha**_, also titled _**Sefer Hamitzvos**_ (Hebrew: דרך מצותך: ספר המצות), is an interpretive work on the Jewish commandments authored by Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn (1789–1866), the third Rebbe of the ChabadHasidic movement. The work is considered a fundamental text of Chabad philosophy.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-bookpage-2)

## Interpretation of the commandments
[edit]
In _Derech Mitzvosecha_, Rabbi Menachem Mendel interprets the Jewish commandments ("mitzvos") according to Kabbalistic and Hasidic teachings. Topics include the commandments of belief in God, prayer, love of a fellow Jew, Tzitzit (fringes on four cornered garments) and Tefillin (phylacteries), and many others.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-bookpage-2) The work provides a Hasidic perspective on fundamental Jewish rites and observances.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-3)
In some cases, Rabbi Menachem Mendel seeks to clarify or reconcile earlier rabbinic interpretations of the commandments, especially where earlier rabbinic authorities disagree on the matter. In this regard, Hasidic interpretations are employed to refine the statements of earlier authorities and/or to clarify or resolve their differences.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-4)

## Interpretation of the commandments
### Love of another Jew
[edit]
In _Derech Mitzvosecha_ Rabbi Menachem Mendel discusses the commandment to love one's fellow and not to hate him/her[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-5) and questions the story in the Talmud concerning Hillel the Elder and the convert. Hillel instructed a non-Jew wishing to convert "what to you is hateful do not do to your friend, this is the (root of) the entire Torah, the rest is commentary. Go and learn."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-6)
For Rabbi Menachem Mendel, the idea of loving one's fellow should only be considered the root of all commandments that relate to human interactions, "between man and his friend" (_bein adam l'chaveiro_), but not to those that are "between man and God" (_bein adam l'makom_).
Rabbi Menachem Mendel resolves this question by introducing the Kabbalistic idea that the souls of the Jewish people compose a "single body"; each individual represents a particular limb.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-7) Based on this concept, every Jew is obligated to love their fellow though the other may have some deficiency, just as the individual often overlooks their own faults due to the natural love one has for one's self. When this kind of "self love" is extended to each other person, it achieves a very strong unity of spirit.
According to Rabbi Menachem Mendel, this unity is representative of the unity between God and the Jewish people and is the root of all the commandments, for aside from the specifics of the individual commandment, each serve the additional function of uniting the Jews with God. Thus each commandment may be said to be the "commentary" of the commandment to love one's fellow.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-8)

## Interpretation of the commandments
### Love of another Jew
Rabbi Menachem Mendel published few of his works during his lifetime. The first edition of _Derech Mitzvosecha_ was in Poltava (current day Ukraine), 1912-1913.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-9) Later editions were published by Kehot Publication Society in Brooklyn, New York.
An English edition of _Derech Mitzvosecha_ was translated by Rabbi Eliyahu Touger and published in 2004 by the Chabad publishing house Sichos in English. The English edition translates selected chapters from Rabbi Schneersohn's work.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-10)
The Kehot editions include a number of appendices in the work, including _Kitzur Tanya_, a summary of the _Tanya_, the classic Chabad work by Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi.

The Chasidic classic Derech Mitzvosecha, by Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Lubavitch also known as the Tzemach Tzedek, the third Lubavitcher Rebbe (5549 [1789] – 5626 [1866]) translated to English.

_**Derech Mitzvosecha**_, also titled _**Sefer Hamitzvos**_ (Hebrew: דרך מצותך: ספר המצות), is an interpretive work on the Jewish commandments authored by Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn (1789–1866), the third Rebbe of the ChabadHasidic movement. The work is considered a fundamental text of Chabad philosophy.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-bookpage-2)

## Interpretation of the commandments
[edit]
In _Derech Mitzvosecha_, Rabbi Menachem Mendel interprets the Jewish commandments ("mitzvos") according to Kabbalistic and Hasidic teachings. Topics include the commandments of belief in God, prayer, love of a fellow Jew, Tzitzit (fringes on four cornered garments) and Tefillin (phylacteries), and many others.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-bookpage-2) The work provides a Hasidic perspective on fundamental Jewish rites and observances.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-3)
In some cases, Rabbi Menachem Mendel seeks to clarify or reconcile earlier rabbinic interpretations of the commandments, especially where earlier rabbinic authorities disagree on the matter. In this regard, Hasidic interpretations are employed to refine the statements of earlier authorities and/or to clarify or resolve their differences.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-4)

## Interpretation of the commandments
### Love of another Jew
[edit]
In _Derech Mitzvosecha_ Rabbi Menachem Mendel discusses the commandment to love one's fellow and not to hate him/her[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-5) and questions the story in the Talmud concerning Hillel the Elder and the convert. Hillel instructed a non-Jew wishing to convert "what to you is hateful do not do to your friend, this is the (root of) the entire Torah, the rest is commentary. Go and learn."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-6)
For Rabbi Menachem Mendel, the idea of loving one's fellow should only be considered the root of all commandments that relate to human interactions, "between man and his friend" (_bein adam l'chaveiro_), but not to those that are "between man and God" (_bein adam l'makom_).
Rabbi Menachem Mendel resolves this question by introducing the Kabbalistic idea that the souls of the Jewish people compose a "single body"; each individual represents a particular limb.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-7) Based on this concept, every Jew is obligated to love their fellow though the other may have some deficiency, just as the individual often overlooks their own faults due to the natural love one has for one's self. When this kind of "self love" is extended to each other person, it achieves a very strong unity of spirit.
According to Rabbi Menachem Mendel, this unity is representative of the unity between God and the Jewish people and is the root of all the commandments, for aside from the specifics of the individual commandment, each serve the additional function of uniting the Jews with God. Thus each commandment may be said to be the "commentary" of the commandment to love one's fellow.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-8)

## Interpretation of the commandments

Rabbi Menachem Mendel published few of his works during his lifetime. The first edition of _Derech Mitzvosecha_ was in Poltava (current day Ukraine), 1912-1913.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-9) Later editions were published by Kehot Publication Society in Brooklyn, New York.
An English edition of _Derech Mitzvosecha_ was translated by Rabbi Eliyahu Touger and published in 2004 by the Chabad publishing house Sichos in English. The English edition translates selected chapters from Rabbi Schneersohn's work.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-10)
The Kehot editions include a number of appendices in the work, including _Kitzur Tanya_, a summary of the _Tanya_, the classic Chabad work by Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi.

R. Menachem Mendel composed this work in his early adulthood. It focuses on many of the 613 mitzvos of the Torah. The Tzemach Tzedek begins his treatment of each mitzvah by quoting the Sefer Hachinuch, the landmark work that lists all 613 mitzvos and their motivating rationales. _**Derech Mitzvosecha**_, also titled _**Sefer Hamitzvos**_ (Hebrew: דרך מצותך: ספר המצות), is an interpretive work on the Jewish commandments authored by Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn (1789–1866), the third Rebbe of the ChabadHasidic movement. The work is considered a fundamental text of Chabad philosophy.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-bookpage-2)

## Interpretation of the commandments
[edit]
In _Derech Mitzvosecha_, Rabbi Menachem Mendel interprets the Jewish commandments ("mitzvos") according to Kabbalistic and Hasidic teachings. Topics include the commandments of belief in God, prayer, love of a fellow Jew, Tzitzit (fringes on four cornered garments) and Tefillin (phylacteries), and many others.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-bookpage-2) The work provides a Hasidic perspective on fundamental Jewish rites and observances.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-3)
In some cases, Rabbi Menachem Mendel seeks to clarify or reconcile earlier rabbinic interpretations of the commandments, especially where earlier rabbinic authorities disagree on the matter. In this regard, Hasidic interpretations are employed to refine the statements of earlier authorities and/or to clarify or resolve their differences.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-4)

## Interpretation of the commandments
### Love of another Jew
[edit]
In _Derech Mitzvosecha_ Rabbi Menachem Mendel discusses the commandment to love one's fellow and not to hate him/her[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-5) and questions the story in the Talmud concerning Hillel the Elder and the convert. Hillel instructed a non-Jew wishing to convert "what to you is hateful do not do to your friend, this is the (root of) the entire Torah, the rest is commentary. Go and learn."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-6)
For Rabbi Menachem Mendel, the idea of loving one's fellow should only be considered the root of all commandments that relate to human interactions, "between man and his friend" (_bein adam l'chaveiro_), but not to those that are "between man and God" (_bein adam l'makom_).
Rabbi Menachem Mendel resolves this question by introducing the Kabbalistic idea that the souls of the Jewish people compose a "single body"; each individual represents a particular limb.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-7) Based on this concept, every Jew is obligated to love their fellow though the other may have some deficiency, just as the individual often overlooks their own faults due to the natural love one has for one's self. When this kind of "self love" is extended to each other person, it achieves a very strong unity of spirit.
According to Rabbi Menachem Mendel, this unity is representative of the unity between God and the Jewish people and is the root of all the commandments, for aside from the specifics of the individual commandment, each serve the additional function of uniting the Jews with God. Thus each commandment may be said to be the "commentary" of the commandment to love one's fellow.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-8)

## Interpretation of the commandments
### Love of another Jew
Rabbi Menachem Mendel published few of his works during his lifetime. The first edition of _Derech Mitzvosecha_ was in Poltava (current day Ukraine), 1912-1913.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-9) Later editions were published by Kehot Publication Society in Brooklyn, New York.
An English edition of _Derech Mitzvosecha_ was translated by Rabbi Eliyahu Touger and published in 2004 by the Chabad publishing house Sichos in English. The English edition translates selected chapters from Rabbi Schneersohn's work.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derech_Mitzvosecha#cite_note-10)
The Kehot editions include a number of appendices in the work, including _Kitzur Tanya_, a summary of the _Tanya_, the classic Chabad work by Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi.

At age 15 he married Sterna Segal, the daughter of Yehuda Leib Segal, a wealthy resident of Vitebsk, and he was then able to devote himself entirely to study.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMindel196910-14) He became an adept in Isaac Luria's system of Kabbalah, and in 1765 he became a disciple of Dov Ber of Mezeritch "the Maggid". Shneur Zalman was a prominent (and the youngest) disciple of _the Maggid_, who was in turn the successor of the founder of Hasidic Judaism, Yisrael ben Eliezer, known as the Baal Shem Tov.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMindel196916%E2%80%9317-15) After returning to his father-in-law's home in _Vitebsk_, he caused a great commotion due to his "conversion" to Hassidism. In 1767, at the age of 22, he was appointed _Maggid_ of Liozna, a position he held until 1801.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMindel196919-16)
According to the Chabad Hasidic tradition, Shneur Zalman's father, Baruch, was a laborer who preferred to earn a living as a gardener rather than accept a post as a community rabbi or as a preacher (_magid_). In this tradition, Baruch was one of the disciples of Rabbi Israel Baal Shem Tov. However, he never—or possibly on rare occasions—joined his teacher on his legendary travels. This tradition is used to justify why Hasidic records do not refer to Baruch with a rabbinic title, claiming that Baruch was averse to any public acknowledgment of his status.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-17)

In the course of the Hasidic movement's establishment, opponents (Misnagdim) arose among the local Jewish communities. Disagreements between Hasidim and their opponents included debates concerning knives used by butchers for _shechita_, and the phrasing of prayers, among others.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-18) In 1772[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-Etkes-19) (or 1775[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMindel196927-20)), Shneur Zalman and a fellow Hasidic leader, Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk (or, according to the tradition in the Soloveitchik family, Levi Yitzchok of Berditchev), attempted to persuade the leader of Lithuanian Jewry, the Vilna Gaon, of the legitimacy of Hasidic practices. However, the _Gaon_ refused to meet with them.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-21)

### Children and succession
[edit]
Shneur Zalman's sons were Dov Ber Schneuri (who eventually succeeded him), Chaim Avraham, and Moshe. Shneur Zalman's daughters were named Freida, Devorah Leah and Rochel.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-Tzetzaim-22)
Dovber Schneuri (1773–1827), named after Shneur Zalman's teacher Dovber of Mezeritch, succeeded his father as Rebbe of the Chabad movement.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-Shneuri-23) When his father died, Shneuri was 39 years old. At the time, he was in the city of Kremenchug.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-cyc-24) Shneuri then moved to the small border-town of Lubavichi, from which the movement would take its name.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-cyc-24) His accession was disputed by one of his father's prime students, Aharon HaLevi of Strashelye, however the majority of Shneur Zalman's followers stayed with Schneuri, and moved to Lubavichi.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-cyc-24) Thus Chabad had now split into two branches, each taking the name of their location to differentiate themselves from each other.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-cyc-24) He established a Yeshiva in Lubavitch, which attracted gifted young scholars. His nephew/son-in-law, Menachem Mendel of Lubavitch, headed the Yeshivah, and later became his successor.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-Shneuri-23)

### Children and succession
Thus, while Schneuri succeeded his father as Rebbe of the Chabad movement, a senior disciple of his father, Aharon HaLevi of Strashelye, a popular and respected figure, differed with him on a number of issues and led a breakaway movement.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-Ehrlich-25)
When Schneur Zalman died, many of his followers flocked to one of his top students, Aharon HaLevi of Strashelye. He had been Shneur Zalman's closest disciple for over thirty years. While many more became followers of Dovber Shneuri, the Strashelye school of Chassidic thought was the subject of many of Dovber's discourses. Aharon HaLevi emphasized the importance of basic emotions in divine service (especially the service of prayer). Dovber Shneuri did not reject the role of emotion in prayer, but emphasized that if the emotion in prayer is to be genuine, it can only be a result of contemplation and understanding (hisbonenus) of the explanations of Chassidus, which in turn will lead to an attainment of "bittul" (self-nullification before the Divine). In his work entitled _Kuntres Hispa'alus_ ("Tract on Ecstasy"), Dovber Shneuri argues that only through ridding oneself of what he considered disingenuous emotions could one attain the ultimate level in Chassidic worship (that is, _bittul_).[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-Ehrlich-25)

### Children and succession
Moshe Schneersohn (born c. 1784 – died, before 1853) was the youngest son of Shneur Zalman. In his early life he was a close student of his father. After his marriage he moved to the town Ulla, Belarus in a Rabbinic position. He suffered with chronic mental illness throughout his life. A trove from the Belarusian archives in Minsk, discovered by Shaul Stampfer reveal documents concerning Moshe being kidnapped and an alleged conversion ceremony. Some scholars have taken this to mean that Moshe converted to Cristianity.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-assaf-26) Other scholars, point to the Catholic Church's investigation into both the alleged conversion and Moshe's mental state, and conclude that the Church itself rejected the conversion as fake and the documents signed by a mentally compromised individual.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-Matusov-27)
During the latter portion of Dovber of Mezeritch's life, his students dispersed over Europe, and after Dovber's death, Shneur Zalman became the leader of Hasidism in Lithuania, along with his senior colleague Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk. When Menachem Mendel died (in 1788), Shneur Zalman was recognized as leader of the Chassidim in Lithuania.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-ReferenceA-28)

### Children and succession
At the time Lithuania was the center of the _Misnagdim_ (opponents of Hasidism), and Shneur Zalman faced much opposition. As mentioned, in 1772, he and Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk traveled to Vilna in an attempt to create a dialogue with the Vilna Gaon who led the Misnagdim and had issued a ban (_cherem_) against the Hasidim, but the Gaon refused to see them (see Vilna Gaon: Antagonism to Hasidism and Hasidim and Mitnagdim).[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMindel196927-20)
Undaunted by the antagonism with the Misnagdim, he succeeded in creating a large network of Hasidic centers. He also joined opposition to Napoleon's advance on Russia by recruiting his disciples to the Czar's army.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMindel1969261_ff-29)
In 1777, Menachem Mendel led a group of approximately 300 Hasidim to immigrate to the Land of Israel. Shneur Zalman attempted to emigrate as well, but was convinced to turn back to Russia so that he could lead Hasidim remaining there while fundraising for emigres.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-30) He was also active in canvassing financial support for the Jewish settlements in the Land of Israel, then under the control of the Ottoman Empire, founding the Colel Chabad charity in 1788.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-31)

### Children and succession
_See Hasidic philosophy_  
As a Talmudist, Shneur Zalman endeavored to place Kabbalah and Hasidism on a rational basis. He chose the name "_Chabad_" for this philosophy—the Hebrewacronym for the intellectual attributes (_sefirot_) _**Ch**ochma_ ("wisdom"), _**B**ina_ ("understanding"), and _[**D**a'at](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Da'at\_(Kabbalah) "Da'at (Kabbalah)")_ ("knowledge"). In his works he "indicated an intelligent and not a blind faith",[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-ReferenceA-28) and assumed an intellectual accessibility of the mystical teachings of the Kabbalah. This intellectual basis differentiates Chabad from other forms of Hasidism – in this context referred to as "_Chagas_"[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-32)—the "emotional" attributes (_sefirot_) of _**Ch**esed_ ("kindness"), _**G**evurah_ ("power"), and _**T**iferes_ ("beauty").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-Dubov,_Pewzner-33) According to Shneur Zalman, a man is neither a static nor a passive entity. He is a dynamic being who must work to develop his potential talent and perfect himself.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-34)
His goal was to make the inner teachings of the Torah, accessible to all, including those of average intelligence, by teaching these lofty concepts in a manner that could be perceived and appreciated by the intellectual mind. The methodology focuses on comprehension and explanation of metaphysical concepts using models, parables, and examples drawn from the human psyche and experience.
Shneur Zalman taught that every Jew is intrinsically bound with God, to the extent that separation is impossible. Chabad Hasidut comprehensibly explores this connection.

**Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn** (Yiddish: מנחם מענדל שניאורסאהן; September 20, 1789 – March 17, 1866), also known as the **Tzemach Tzedek** (Hebrew: "Righteous Sprout" or "Righteous Scion"), was an Orthodoxrabbi, leading 19th-century posek, and the third Rebbe (spiritual leader) of the Chabad LubavitchHasidic movement.

Menachem Mendel Schneersohn was born in Liozna, on September 20, 1789 (September 9 OS). His mother Devorah Leah died three years later, and her father Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi raised him as his own son. He married his first cousin Chaya Mushka Schneersohn, daughter of Rabbi Dovber Schneuri. After his father-in-law/uncle's death, and a three-year interregnum during which he tried to persuade the Hasidim to accept his brother-in-law Menachem-Nachum Schneuri or his uncle Chaim-Avraham as their leader,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1) he assumed the leadership of Lubavitch on the eve of Shavuot 5591 (May 5, 1831, OS).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-2)
He was known as the Tzemach Tzedek after the title of a voluminous compendium of Halakha (Jewish law) that he authored.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-3) He also authored _Derech Mitzvotecha_ ("Way of Your Commandments"), a mystical exposition of the _Mitzvos_. He compiled major works of Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi for publication, including the _Siddur L'Kol Ha'Shanah_ (commonly known as _Siddur Im Dach_), _Likutei Torah_ and _Torah Ohr_. He also authored a philosophical text entitled _Sefer HaChakira: Derech Emunah_ (_Book of Philosophy: The Way of Faith_).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-4)

He enjoyed close ties with other Jewish leaders. In the course of his battle against the _Haskalah_ in Russia, he forged a close alliance with Rabbi Yitzchak of Valozhyn, a major leader of the misnagdim, which led to warmer relations between them and the Hasidim.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-5)
According to Baruch Epstein, his father Rabbi Yechiel Michel Epstein spent six months under the Schneersohn's tutelage, and learned most of his mystical knowledge during that time. This story is disputed by Hassidic historian Yehoshua Mondshine.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-6) Historian [Eitam Henkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_Eitam_and_Na'ama_Henkin "Murder of Eitam and Na'ama Henkin") suggests that Rabbi Y. M. Epstein did meet with him, but only a few visits over a week or two, noting the testimony of Rabbi Yehuda Leib Maimon that he heard about this directly from his teacher.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-7)
His close friendship with Professor J Berstenson, the Czar's court physician, often helped the delicate negotiations relating to the welfare of the community.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1) He set up an organisation called _Hevras Techiyas Hameisim_ to assist Jewish boy-soldiers who were being recruited and converted to Christianity by the Russian army. These soldiers known as Cantonists were taken away from the Jewish community to other villages. Schneersohn arranged for his students to pay them regular visits to keep up their spirits and discourage them from converting.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1)

In 1844–45 he took steps to increase the enrollment and viability of the Lubavitch yeshivas in Dubroŭna, Pasana, Lyozno, and Kalisz, expanding their enrollment to around 600 students in total.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-8) Repeated attempts by the authorities to entrap him using informers such as Hershel Hodesh, Benjamin the Apostate and Lipman Feldman failed.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-9)
He died in Lubavitch on March 17, 1866, at the age of 76, leaving seven sons. He was succeeded by his youngest son, Shmuel[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1) as the Rebbe of Lubavitch, while several other sons established separate Chabad branches, including Kopust, Liadi, Niezhin and Avrutch.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-hayom-yom-intro-10)
Several of his sons established Chasidic dynasties.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1)
He had seven sons:[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-hayom-yom-intro-10)

**Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn** (Yiddish: מנחם מענדל שניאורסאהן; September 20, 1789 – March 17, 1866), also known as the **Tzemach Tzedek** (Hebrew: "Righteous Sprout" or "Righteous Scion"), was an Orthodoxrabbi, leading 19th-century posek, and the third Rebbe (spiritual leader) of the Chabad LubavitchHasidic movement.
texts.1:
Menachem Mendel Schneersohn was born in Liozna, on September 20, 1789 (September 9 OS). His mother Devorah Leah died three years later, and her father Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi raised him as his own son. He married his first cousin Chaya Mushka Schneersohn, daughter of Rabbi Dovber Schneuri. After his father-in-law/uncle's death, and a three-year interregnum during which he tried to persuade the Hasidim to accept his brother-in-law Menachem-Nachum Schneuri or his uncle Chaim-Avraham as their leader,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1) he assumed the leadership of Lubavitch on the eve of Shavuot 5591 (May 5, 1831, OS).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-2)
He was known as the Tzemach Tzedek after the title of a voluminous compendium of Halakha (Jewish law) that he authored.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-3) He also authored _Derech Mitzvotecha_ ("Way of Your Commandments"), a mystical exposition of the _Mitzvos_. He compiled major works of Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi for publication, including the _Siddur L'Kol Ha'Shanah_ (commonly known as _Siddur Im Dach_), _Likutei Torah_ and _Torah Ohr_. He also authored a philosophical text entitled _Sefer HaChakira: Derech Emunah_ (_Book of Philosophy: The Way of Faith_).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-4)
texts.2:
He enjoyed close ties with other Jewish leaders. In the course of his battle against the _Haskalah_ in Russia, he forged a close alliance with Rabbi Yitzchak of Valozhyn, a major leader of the misnagdim, which led to warmer relations between them and the Hasidim.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-5)
According to Baruch Epstein, his father Rabbi Yechiel Michel Epstein spent six months under the Schneersohn's tutelage, and learned most of his mystical knowledge during that time. This story is disputed by Hassidic historian Yehoshua Mondshine.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-6) Historian [Eitam Henkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_Eitam_and_Na'ama_Henkin "Murder of Eitam and Na'ama Henkin") suggests that Rabbi Y. M. Epstein did meet with him, but only a few visits over a week or two, noting the testimony of Rabbi Yehuda Leib Maimon that he heard about this directly from his teacher.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-7)
His close friendship with Professor J Berstenson, the Czar's court physician, often helped the delicate negotiations relating to the welfare of the community.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1) He set up an organisation called _Hevras Techiyas Hameisim_ to assist Jewish boy-soldiers who were being recruited and converted to Christianity by the Russian army. These soldiers known as Cantonists were taken away from the Jewish community to other villages. Schneersohn arranged for his students to pay them regular visits to keep up their spirits and discourage them from converting.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1)
texts.3:
In 1844–45 he took steps to increase the enrollment and viability of the Lubavitch yeshivas in Dubroŭna, Pasana, Lyozno, and Kalisz, expanding their enrollment to around 600 students in total.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-8) Repeated attempts by the authorities to entrap him using informers such as Hershel Hodesh, Benjamin the Apostate and Lipman Feldman failed.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-9)
He died in Lubavitch on March 17, 1866, at the age of 76, leaving seven sons. He was succeeded by his youngest son, Shmuel[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1) as the Rebbe of Lubavitch, while several other sons established separate Chabad branches, including Kopust, Liadi, Niezhin and Avrutch.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-hayom-yom-intro-10)
Several of his sons established Chasidic dynasties.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1)
He had seven sons:[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-hayom-yom-intro-10)

At age 15 he married Sterna Segal, the daughter of Yehuda Leib Segal, a wealthy resident of Vitebsk, and he was then able to devote himself entirely to study.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMindel196910-14) He became an adept in Isaac Luria's system of Kabbalah, and in 1765 he became a disciple of Dov Ber of Mezeritch "the Maggid". Shneur Zalman was a prominent (and the youngest) disciple of _the Maggid_, who was in turn the successor of the founder of Hasidic Judaism, Yisrael ben Eliezer, known as the Baal Shem Tov.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMindel196916%E2%80%9317-15) After returning to his father-in-law's home in _Vitebsk_, he caused a great commotion due to his "conversion" to Hassidism. In 1767, at the age of 22, he was appointed _Maggid_ of Liozna, a position he held until 1801.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMindel196919-16)
According to the Chabad Hasidic tradition, Shneur Zalman's father, Baruch, was a laborer who preferred to earn a living as a gardener rather than accept a post as a community rabbi or as a preacher (_magid_). In this tradition, Baruch was one of the disciples of Rabbi Israel Baal Shem Tov. However, he never—or possibly on rare occasions—joined his teacher on his legendary travels. This tradition is used to justify why Hasidic records do not refer to Baruch with a rabbinic title, claiming that Baruch was averse to any public acknowledgment of his status.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-17)
texts.4: In the course of the Hasidic movement's establishment, opponents (Misnagdim) arose among the local Jewish communities. Disagreements between Hasidim and their opponents included debates concerning knives used by butchers for _shechita_, and the phrasing of prayers, among others.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-18) In 1772[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-Etkes-19) (or 1775[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMindel196927-20)), Shneur Zalman and a fellow Hasidic leader, Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk (or, according to the tradition in the Soloveitchik family, Levi Yitzchok of Berditchev), attempted to persuade the leader of Lithuanian Jewry, the Vilna Gaon, of the legitimacy of Hasidic practices. However, the _Gaon_ refused to meet with them.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-21)

### Children and succession
[edit]
Shneur Zalman's sons were Dov Ber Schneuri (who eventually succeeded him), Chaim Avraham, and Moshe. Shneur Zalman's daughters were named Freida, Devorah Leah and Rochel.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-Tzetzaim-22)
Dovber Schneuri (1773–1827), named after Shneur Zalman's teacher Dovber of Mezeritch, succeeded his father as Rebbe of the Chabad movement.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-Shneuri-23) When his father died, Shneuri was 39 years old. At the time, he was in the city of Kremenchug.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-cyc-24) Shneuri then moved to the small border-town of Lubavichi, from which the movement would take its name.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-cyc-24) His accession was disputed by one of his father's prime students, Aharon HaLevi of Strashelye, however the majority of Shneur Zalman's followers stayed with Schneuri, and moved to Lubavichi.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-cyc-24) Thus Chabad had now split into two branches, each taking the name of their location to differentiate themselves from each other.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-cyc-24) He established a Yeshiva in Lubavitch, which attracted gifted young scholars. His nephew/son-in-law, Menachem Mendel of Lubavitch, headed the Yeshivah, and later became his successor.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-Shneuri-23)
texts.6:
### Children and succession
Thus, while Schneuri succeeded his father as Rebbe of the Chabad movement, a senior disciple of his father, Aharon HaLevi of Strashelye, a popular and respected figure, differed with him on a number of issues and led a breakaway movement.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-Ehrlich-25)
When Schneur Zalman died, many of his followers flocked to one of his top students, Aharon HaLevi of Strashelye. He had been Shneur Zalman's closest disciple for over thirty years. While many more became followers of Dovber Shneuri, the Strashelye school of Chassidic thought was the subject of many of Dovber's discourses. Aharon HaLevi emphasized the importance of basic emotions in divine service (especially the service of prayer). Dovber Shneuri did not reject the role of emotion in prayer, but emphasized that if the emotion in prayer is to be genuine, it can only be a result of contemplation and understanding (hisbonenus) of the explanations of Chassidus, which in turn will lead to an attainment of "bittul" (self-nullification before the Divine). In his work entitled _Kuntres Hispa'alus_ ("Tract on Ecstasy"), Dovber Shneuri argues that only through ridding oneself of what he considered disingenuous emotions could one attain the ultimate level in Chassidic worship (that is, _bittul_).[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-Ehrlich-25)
texts.7:
### Children and succession
Moshe Schneersohn (born c. 1784 – died, before 1853) was the youngest son of Shneur Zalman. In his early life he was a close student of his father. After his marriage he moved to the town Ulla, Belarus in a Rabbinic position. He suffered with chronic mental illness throughout his life. A trove from the Belarusian archives in Minsk, discovered by Shaul Stampfer reveal documents concerning Moshe being kidnapped and an alleged conversion ceremony. Some scholars have taken this to mean that Moshe converted to Cristianity.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-assaf-26) Other scholars, point to the Catholic Church's investigation into both the alleged conversion and Moshe's mental state, and conclude that the Church itself rejected the conversion as fake and the documents signed by a mentally compromised individual.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-Matusov-27)
During the latter portion of Dovber of Mezeritch's life, his students dispersed over Europe, and after Dovber's death, Shneur Zalman became the leader of Hasidism in Lithuania, along with his senior colleague Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk. When Menachem Mendel died (in 1788), Shneur Zalman was recognized as leader of the Chassidim in Lithuania.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-ReferenceA-28)
texts.8:
### Children and succession
At the time Lithuania was the center of the _Misnagdim_ (opponents of Hasidism), and Shneur Zalman faced much opposition. As mentioned, in 1772, he and Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk traveled to Vilna in an attempt to create a dialogue with the Vilna Gaon who led the Misnagdim and had issued a ban (_cherem_) against the Hasidim, but the Gaon refused to see them (see Vilna Gaon: Antagonism to Hasidism and Hasidim and Mitnagdim).[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMindel196927-20)
Undaunted by the antagonism with the Misnagdim, he succeeded in creating a large network of Hasidic centers. He also joined opposition to Napoleon's advance on Russia by recruiting his disciples to the Czar's army.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMindel1969261_ff-29)
In 1777, Menachem Mendel led a group of approximately 300 Hasidim to immigrate to the Land of Israel. As a Talmudist, Shneur Zalman endeavored to place Kabbalah and Hasidism on a rational basis. He chose the name "_Chabad_" for this philosophy—the Hebrewacronym for the intellectual attributes (_sefirot_) _**Ch**ochma_ ("wisdom"), _**B**ina_ ("understanding"), and _[**D**a'at](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Da'at\_(Kabbalah) "Da'at (Kabbalah)")_ ("knowledge"). This intellectual basis differentiates Chabad from other forms of Hasidism – in this context referred to as "_Chagas_"[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-32)—the "emotional" attributes (_sefirot_) of _**Ch**esed_ ("kindness"), _**G**evurah_ ("power"), and _**T**iferes_ ("beauty").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-Dubov,_Pewzner-33) According to Shneur Zalman, a man is neither a static nor a passive entity. He is a dynamic being who must work to develop his potential talent and perfect himself.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-34)
His goal was to make the inner teachings of the Torah, accessible to all, including those of average intelligence, by teaching these lofty concepts in a manner that could be perceived and appreciated by the intellectual mind. The methodology focuses on comprehension and explanation of metaphysical concepts using models, parables, and examples drawn from the human psyche and experience.
Shneur Zalman taught that every Jew is intrinsically bound with God, to the extent that separation is impossible. Chabad Hasidut comprehensibly explores this connection.

**Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneersohn** (Yiddish: מנחם מענדל שניאורסאהן; September 20, 1789 – March 17, 1866), also known as the **Tzemach Tzedek** (Hebrew: "Righteous Sprout" or "Righteous Scion"), was an Orthodoxrabbi, leading 19th-century posek, and the third Rebbe (spiritual leader) of the Chabad LubavitchHasidic movement.

Menachem Mendel Schneersohn was born in Liozna, on September 20, 1789 (September 9 OS). His mother Devorah Leah died three years later, and her father Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi raised him as his own son. He married his first cousin Chaya Mushka Schneersohn, daughter of Rabbi Dovber Schneuri. After his father-in-law/uncle's death, and a three-year interregnum during which he tried to persuade the Hasidim to accept his brother-in-law Menachem-Nachum Schneuri or his uncle Chaim-Avraham as their leader,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1) he assumed the leadership of Lubavitch on the eve of Shavuot 5591 (May 5, 1831, OS).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-2)
He was known as the Tzemach Tzedek after the title of a voluminous compendium of Halakha (Jewish law) that he authored.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-3) He also authored _Derech Mitzvotecha_ ("Way of Your Commandments"), a mystical exposition of the _Mitzvos_. He compiled major works of Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi for publication, including the _Siddur L'Kol Ha'Shanah_ (commonly known as _Siddur Im Dach_), _Likutei Torah_ and _Torah Ohr_. He also authored a philosophical text entitled _Sefer HaChakira: Derech Emunah_ (_Book of Philosophy: The Way of Faith_).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-4)

He enjoyed close ties with other Jewish leaders. In the course of his battle against the _Haskalah_ in Russia, he forged a close alliance with Rabbi Yitzchak of Valozhyn, a major leader of the misnagdim, which led to warmer relations between them and the Hasidim.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-5)
According to Baruch Epstein, his father Rabbi Yechiel Michel Epstein spent six months under the Schneersohn's tutelage, and learned most of his mystical knowledge during that time. This story is disputed by Hassidic historian Yehoshua Mondshine.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-6) Historian [Eitam Henkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_Eitam_and_Na'ama_Henkin "Murder of Eitam and Na'ama Henkin") suggests that Rabbi Y. M. His close friendship with Professor J Berstenson, the Czar's court physician, often helped the delicate negotiations relating to the welfare of the community.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menachem_Mendel_Schneersohn#cite_note-poor-1) He set up an organisation called _Hevras Techiyas Hameisim_ to assist Jewish boy-soldiers who were being recruited and converted to Christianity by the Russian army. At age 15 he married Sterna Segal, the daughter of Yehuda Leib Segal, a wealthy resident of Vitebsk, and he was then able to devote himself entirely to study.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMindel196910-14) He became an adept in Isaac Luria's system of Kabbalah, and in 1765 he became a disciple of Dov Ber of Mezeritch "the Maggid". Shneur Zalman was a prominent (and the youngest) disciple of _the Maggid_, who was in turn the successor of the founder of Hasidic Judaism, Yisrael ben Eliezer, known as the Baal Shem Tov.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMindel196916%E2%80%9317-15) After returning to his father-in-law's home in _Vitebsk_, he caused a great commotion due to his "conversion" to Hassidism. In 1767, at the age of 22, he was appointed _Maggid_ of Liozna, a position he held until 1801.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMindel196919-16)
According to the Chabad Hasidic tradition, Shneur Zalman's father, Baruch, was a laborer who preferred to earn a living as a gardener rather than accept a post as a community rabbi or as a preacher (_magid_). In this tradition, Baruch was one of the disciples of Rabbi Israel Baal Shem Tov. However, he never—or possibly on rare occasions—joined his teacher on his legendary travels. This tradition is used to justify why Hasidic records do not refer to Baruch with a rabbinic title, claiming that Baruch was averse to any public acknowledgment of his status.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-17)

In the course of the Hasidic movement's establishment, opponents (Misnagdim) arose among the local Jewish communities. Disagreements between Hasidim and their opponents included debates concerning knives used by butchers for _shechita_, and the phrasing of prayers, among others.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-18) In 1772[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-Etkes-19) (or 1775[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMindel196927-20)), Shneur Zalman and a fellow Hasidic leader, Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk (or, according to the tradition in the Soloveitchik family, Levi Yitzchok of Berditchev), attempted to persuade the leader of Lithuanian Jewry, the Vilna Gaon, of the legitimacy of Hasidic practices. However, the _Gaon_ refused to meet with them.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-21)

### Children and succession
[edit]
Shneur Zalman's sons were Dov Ber Schneuri (who eventually succeeded him), Chaim Avraham, and Moshe. Shneur Zalman's daughters were named Freida, Devorah Leah and Rochel.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-Tzetzaim-22)
Dovber Schneuri (1773–1827), named after Shneur Zalman's teacher Dovber of Mezeritch, succeeded his father as Rebbe of the Chabad movement.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-Shneuri-23) When his father died, Shneuri was 39 years old. At the time, he was in the city of Kremenchug.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-cyc-24) Shneuri then moved to the small border-town of Lubavichi, from which the movement would take its name.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-cyc-24) His accession was disputed by one of his father's prime students, Aharon HaLevi of Strashelye, however the majority of Shneur Zalman's followers stayed with Schneuri, and moved to Lubavichi.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-cyc-24) Thus Chabad had now split into two branches, each taking the name of their location to differentiate themselves from each other.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-cyc-24) He established a Yeshiva in Lubavitch, which attracted gifted young scholars. His nephew/son-in-law, Menachem Mendel of Lubavitch, headed the Yeshivah, and later became his successor.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-Shneuri-23)

### Children and succession
Thus, while Schneuri succeeded his father as Rebbe of the Chabad movement, a senior disciple of his father, Aharon HaLevi of Strashelye, a popular and respected figure, differed with him on a number of issues and led a breakaway movement.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-Ehrlich-25)
When Schneur Zalman died, many of his followers flocked to one of his top students, Aharon HaLevi of Strashelye. He had been Shneur Zalman's closest disciple for over thirty years. While many more became followers of Dovber Shneuri, the Strashelye school of Chassidic thought was the subject of many of Dovber's discourses. Aharon HaLevi emphasized the importance of basic emotions in divine service (especially the service of prayer). Dovber Shneuri did not reject the role of emotion in prayer, but emphasized that if the emotion in prayer is to be genuine, it can only be a result of contemplation and understanding (hisbonenus) of the explanations of Chassidus, which in turn will lead to an attainment of "bittul" (self-nullification before the Divine). In his work entitled _Kuntres Hispa'alus_ ("Tract on Ecstasy"), Dovber Shneuri argues that only through ridding oneself of what he considered disingenuous emotions could one attain the ultimate level in Chassidic worship (that is, _bittul_).[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-Ehrlich-25)

### Children and succession
Moshe Schneersohn (born c. 1784 – died, before 1853) was the youngest son of Shneur Zalman. In his early life he was a close student of his father. After his marriage he moved to the town Ulla, Belarus in a Rabbinic position. He suffered with chronic mental illness throughout his life. A trove from the Belarusian archives in Minsk, discovered by Shaul Stampfer reveal documents concerning Moshe being kidnapped and an alleged conversion ceremony. Some scholars have taken this to mean that Moshe converted to Cristianity.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-assaf-26) Other scholars, point to the Catholic Church's investigation into both the alleged conversion and Moshe's mental state, and conclude that the Church itself rejected the conversion as fake and the documents signed by a mentally compromised individual.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-Matusov-27)
During the latter portion of Dovber of Mezeritch's life, his students dispersed over Europe, and after Dovber's death, Shneur Zalman became the leader of Hasidism in Lithuania, along with his senior colleague Menachem Mendel of Vitebsk. When Menachem Mendel died (in 1788), Shneur Zalman was recognized as leader of the Chassidim in Lithuania.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shneur_Zalman_of_Liadi#cite_note-ReferenceA-28)

His goal was to make the inner teachings of the Torah, accessible to all, including those of average intelligence, by teaching these lofty concepts in a manner that could be perceived and appreciated by the intellectual mind. The methodology focuses on comprehension and explanation of metaphysical concepts using models, parables, and examples drawn from the human psyche and experience.
Shneur Zalman taught that every Jew is intrinsically bound with God, to the extent that separation is impossible. Chabad Hasidut comprehensibly explores this connection.

**Menachem Mendel Schneersohn – the third Rebbe of Chabad and author of *Derech Mitzvosecha* – followed the teachings and example of his father‑figure and mentor, Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi.**  

- Shneur Zalman was the founder of the Chabad‑Lubavitch Hasidic movement and the great‑grandfather’s teacher.  
- Schneersohn was raised by Shneur Zalman after his mother died and studied under him, taking to heart Shneur’s Chabad philosophy (“Chabad” = Chochma‑Bina‑Da’at).  
- In his own writings, Schneersohn repeatedly cites the *Tanya* and other works compiled by Shneur Zalman, showing that he followed and built upon his mentor’s ideas.  

So, the creator of *Derech Mitzvosecha* followed **Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi**.
